definition: So distinctive or excellent that no one else can copy it.
example: The museum guide spoke with an inimitable blend of dry humor and deep expertise.
nuance: Inimitable stresses that others cannot copy something, while unique only says there is one; it is unrelated to inimical, meaning hostile.
prompt: A beloved jazz singer gives her farewell concert after forty years on stage.
options: Critics praised her inimitable phrasing, which students had tried and failed to copy.
Her inimitable phrasing was so ordinary that any student in the hall could reproduce it.
The inimitable crowd booed loudly, hostile to every song she chose to perform.
Her inimitable encore was certain to happen, since she had closed every show with one.
reasons: A style that many attempt to reproduce but none can match is exactly what the word describes.
Something easy to copy is the reverse of a style no one can match.
This confuses the word with inimical, which means unfriendly or hostile.
This mixes the word up with inevitable; being certain to occur has nothing to do with being uncopyable.

practice.prompt: A family gathers on a winter night to hear a grandfather tell his famous stories.
options: His inimitable tale that night was copied straight from a magazine he had read last week.
Cousins tried his inimitable timing, but no one could pause quite the way he did.
His inimitable stories were simple to retell, so everyone told them just as well as he did.
His inimitable glare made the grandchildren feel unwelcome at the dinner table.
reasons: A borrowed, copied story is derivative, the opposite of something no one can reproduce.
Others attempting his delivery and falling short shows it truly cannot be copied.
If anyone can match the performance, it is not beyond imitation.
The word praises matchless quality; it does not mean unfriendly, which would be inimical.
